newsitem.title: CANADA: Hibernia partners to build Newfoundland oil terminal.
newsitem.headline: Hibernia partners to build Newfoundland oil terminal.

text.p: Three major partners in the C$6.2-billion ($4.5-billion) Hibernia oil project off the east coast of Canada said Thursday they will build a major crude oil terminal in the Atlantic province of Newfoundland.

The so-called transshipment terminal will be designed to take in oil produced from the Hibernia project and will likely be expanded later to handle output from several other future offshore projects, Petro-Canada and the Canadian units of Mobil Corp. and Chevron Corp. said.
The project is expected to cost more than C$100 million ($73 million) to accommodate Hibernia's requirements.
The 1.5-million-barrel heated facility, which would initially include one berth for oil tankers will be built at Whiffin Head on Newfoundland's eastern Avalon Peninsula.
At least two more berths could be added in the future.
Transshipment is a two-stage transport process for moving oil to market. Oil from offshore production facilities is tranferred to shuttle tankers, which carry it to the terminal.
The crude is stored at the transshipment facility until it is loaded on a conventional tanker and shipped to markets.
The partners said the terminal's eventual expansion would be a welcome addition for future oil projects planned for the Grand Banks off Canada's east coast.

"Three of the (Hibernia) partners, Mobil, Chevron and Petro-Canada, have multiple interests on the Grand Banks and our evaluation showed that a transshipment facility closest to the point of production made the most sense for us from an economic standpoint," said Jerry Anderson, president of Mobil unit Mobil Oil Canada.
Newfoundland Premier Brian Tobin, whose province's economy was devastated by the 1992 collapse of its fishing industry, said renewed oil activity in the region was aiding a recovery.

Also on Thursday, Mobil, Chevron and another Hibernia partner, Murphy Oil Corp., said they chose St. John's, Newfoundland-based Canship Ugland Ltd., a Canadian-Norwegian consortium, to manage shuttle tanker operations for the project.

Under the deal, expected to cost Hibernia C$8 million ($5.8 million) a year, Canship Ugland would be responsible for supplying the tanker crew, repair and maintenance and administration for the vessel.
The ship, to be called the Motor Tanker Kometik, was being constructed by Samsung Heavy Industries in Korea.
Partners in Hibernia are Petro-Canada with 25 percent, Mobil with 33.125 percent, Chevron with 26.875 percent, Murphy with 6.5 percent and the government of Canada with 8.5 percent.
